title: Part 2, Chapter 53
paragraphs: Of the troubled end and conclusion that Sancho Panza’s government came to

To imagine that anything in this life will stay forever in the same state is an idle dream; on the contrary, everything here seems to move in a circle — round and round, I mean. Spring gives way to summer, summer to the fall, the fall to autumn, autumn to winter, and winter to spring again, and so time keeps turning on its never-resting wheel. Only human life, swifter than time itself, races toward its end with no hope of renewal, except in that other life which has no limit and no boundary. So says Cide Hamete, the Mohammedan philosopher; for there are many who, by the light of nature alone and without the light of faith, have grasped the fleetingness and instability of this present life and the endless duration of the eternal life we hope for. But our author is speaking here of the speed with which Sancho’s government ended, melted away, disappeared — vanished, as it were, into smoke and shadow. As Sancho lay in bed on the night of the seventh day of his governorship, sated not with bread and wine but with handing down judgments, giving opinions, and issuing laws and proclamations, sleep — in spite of his hunger — was just beginning to close his eyelids when he heard such a din of bell-ringing and shouting that you would have thought the whole island was going under. He sat up in bed and listened intently, trying to work out what could be causing so great an uproar; but not only could he not discover it — when countless drums and trumpets joined the clamor of the bells and shouts, he grew more bewildered than ever, and was filled with fear and dread. Getting up, he put on a pair of slippers because the floor was damp, and without throwing on a dressing gown or anything of the sort he rushed out the door of his room, just in time to see more than twenty people coming along a corridor with lighted torches and drawn swords in their hands, all shouting, “To arms, to arms, señor governor, to arms! The enemy has landed on the island in countless numbers, and we are lost unless your skill and courage come to our rescue.”

Keeping up this noise, commotion, and uproar, they came to where Sancho stood stunned and bewildered by everything he was seeing and hearing, and as they drew near one of them shouted to him, “Arm yourself at once, your lordship, unless you want to be destroyed and the whole island lost with you.”

“What business do I have with arming?” said Sancho. “What do I know about weapons or rescues? Better to leave all that to my master Don Quixote, who will settle it and make everything safe in an instant; for I, sinner that I am, God help me, understand nothing about these brawls.”

“Ah, señor governor,” said another, “what faintheartedness is this! Arm yourself; here are arms for you, offensive and defensive alike; come out to the plaza and be our leader and captain — it falls to you by right, since you are our governor.”

“Arm me, then, in God’s name,” said Sancho, and they immediately produced two large shields they had brought along and strapped them onto him over his shirt, without letting him put on anything else — one shield in front and the other behind — and passing his arms through openings they had cut, they bound him tight with ropes, so that there he stood, walled and boarded in, straight as a spindle, unable to bend his knees or move a single step. They put a lance in his hand, which he leaned on to keep himself from falling, and as soon as they had him rigged out like this they ordered him to march forward, lead them on, and put courage into them all; for with him as their guide, their lamp, and their morning star, they were certain to bring the business to a happy conclusion.

“And how am I supposed to march, unlucky creature that I am,” said Sancho, “when I can’t move my kneecaps, because these boards tied so tight against my body won’t let me? What you’ll have to do is carry me in your arms and lay me across some postern gate, or stand me upright in one, and I’ll hold it either with this lance or with my own body.”

“On with you, señor governor!” cried another. “It’s fear more than the boards that keeps you from moving. Hurry up, get yourself going, for there’s no time to lose; the enemy is growing in numbers, the shouting is getting louder, and the danger is pressing in.”

Spurred on by these urgings and reproaches, the poor governor made an attempt to move forward — and fell to the ground with such a crash that he thought he had smashed himself to pieces. There he lay, like a tortoise shut up inside its shell, or a side of bacon pressed between two kneading-troughs, or a boat turned bottom-up on the beach; and the gang of pranksters felt no pity at all when they saw him fall. Far from it: putting out their torches, they began shouting again and renewing the calls to arms with such fury — trampling over poor Sancho and slashing at him over the shields with their swords — that if he had not pulled himself together, made himself small, and drawn his head in between the shields, things would have gone very badly for the poor governor. Squeezed into that narrow space, he lay there sweating and sweating again, commending himself with all his heart to God to deliver him from this peril. Some stumbled over him, others fell on top of him, and one man actually planted himself on top of him for a good while, and from there, as if from a watchtower, gave orders to the troops, shouting, “Over here, our men! The enemy is thickest here! Hold that breach! Shut that gate! Barricade those ladders! Bring up the stink-pots of pitch and resin, and the kettles of boiling oil! Block the streets with feather beds!” In short, in his zeal he named every little thing, every implement and engine of war used to beat back an assault on a city, while the bruised and battered Sancho, who heard it all and suffered it all, kept saying to himself, “O, if it would only please the Lord to let the island fall this instant, so that I could find myself dead or out of this torment!” Heaven heard his prayer, and when he least expected it he heard voices crying, “Victory, victory! The enemy is beaten and retreating! Come, señor governor — get up, come enjoy the victory and divide the spoils won from the foe by the might of that invincible arm.”

“Lift me up,” said the miserable Sancho in a doleful voice. They helped him to his feet, and once he was standing he said, “The enemy I’ve beaten you can nail to my forehead. I don’t want to divide any spoils of the foe; all I beg and entreat of some friend, if I have one, is a swallow of wine, because I’m parched with thirst — and wipe me dry, because I’m dissolving into water.”

They rubbed him down, brought him wine, and untied the shields, and he sat down on his bed and, what with fear, agitation, and exhaustion, fainted away. The people who had been in on the joke were sorry now that they had pushed it so far; but the alarm his fainting had caused them was eased when he came back to himself. He asked what time it was; they told him day was just breaking. He said nothing more and began to dress in silence, while everyone watched him, waiting to see what this hurry to get his clothes on could mean.

At last he was dressed, and then — slowly, for he was badly bruised and could not move quickly — he made his way to the stable, followed by everyone present. Going up to Dapple, he embraced him, gave him a loving kiss on the forehead, and said, not without tears in his eyes, “Come along, my comrade and friend, partner in my labors and sorrows. When I was with you, and had no cares beyond mending your harness and feeding your little body, my hours, my days, and my years were happy ones; but since I left you and climbed the towers of ambition and pride, a thousand miseries, a thousand troubles, and four thousand anxieties have entered my soul.” And all the while he was talking this way he was strapping the pack-saddle onto the ass, without anyone saying a word. Then, with Dapple saddled, he climbed onto him with great pain and difficulty, and addressing the majordomo, the secretary, the head carver, Pedro Recio the doctor, and several others standing by, he said, “Make way, gentlemen, and let me go back to my old freedom; let me go find my former life, and raise myself up out of this present death. I was not born to be a governor, or to defend islands or cities from whatever enemies choose to attack them. Plowing and digging, dressing and pruning vines, suit me better than defending provinces or kingdoms. Saint Peter is fine in Rome — I mean, each of us is best off at the trade he was born to. A reaping-hook sits better in my hand than a governor’s scepter. I’d rather eat my fill of gazpacho than be at the mercy of a meddling doctor who kills me with hunger; and I’d rather stretch out in summer under the shade of an oak, and wrap myself in winter in a double sheepskin jacket, in freedom, than lie between holland sheets and dress in sables under the burden of a government. God be with your worships, and tell my lord the duke that ‘naked I was born, naked I find myself; I neither lose nor gain’ — I mean that I came into this government without a penny and I leave it without a penny, which is very different from how governors usually depart from other islands. Now stand aside and let me go; I have to plaster myself up, because I believe every one of my ribs is crushed, thanks to the enemies who have been walking all over me tonight.”

“There is no need for that, señor governor,” said Doctor Recio, “for I will give your worship a draught against falls and bruises that will soon make you as sound and strong as ever; and as for your diet, I promise your worship to mend my ways and let you eat your fill of whatever you like.”

“You speak too late,” said Sancho. “I’d as soon turn Turk as stay here any longer. These jokes won’t work a second time. By God, I’d no more remain in this government, or accept another one — even if it were served up to me between two plates — than I’d fly to heaven without wings. I’m of the breed of the Panzas, and every one of them is stubborn: once they say ‘odds,’ odds it has to be, even if it turns out evens, no matter what the world says. Here in this stable I leave behind the ant’s wings that carried me up into the air for the swifts and the other birds to eat me; let’s get back to level ground and our own two feet — and if they aren’t shod in fancy pinked shoes of cordovan leather, they won’t lack for rough hempen sandals. ‘Every ewe to her own kind,’ and ‘let no one stretch his leg further than the sheet reaches’; and now let me pass, for it’s getting late for me.”

To this the majordomo replied, “Señor governor, we would let your worship go with all our hearts, though it grieves us deeply to lose you, for your wit and your Christian conduct naturally make us sorry to part with you. But everyone knows that a governor, before leaving the place he has governed, is obliged first of all to render an account. Let your worship give one for the ten days you have held the government, and then go, and the peace of God go with you.”

“No one can demand that of me,” said Sancho, “except whoever my lord the duke appoints; and I’m on my way to see him now, and to him I will render an exact account. Besides, when I leave as naked as I do, no other proof is needed to show that I have governed like an angel.”
“By God, the great Sancho is right,” said Doctor Recio, “and we ought to let him go, for the duke will be delighted beyond measure to see him.”

They all agreed and let him go, first offering to keep him company and to supply him with anything he might want for his own comfort or for the journey. Sancho said he wanted nothing more than a little barley for Dapple and half a cheese and half a loaf of bread for himself; the distance was so short that there was no need for better or more abundant provisions. They all embraced him, and he, in tears, embraced every one of them, and left them marveling not only at his words but at his firm and sensible resolution.
